global-agriculture-s1.title: A global supply chain for bananas

image.alt: Seven boxes joined by arrows: a farm in Ecuador, a packing house where fruit is washed and boxed, the port of Guayaquil, a refrigerated ship kept at about 13 degrees Celsius, a port in the United States, a ripening center where gas ripens the fruit, and a store where a shopper buys it. The first three steps are in the exporting country and the last three in the importing country. Each step adds cost and value, and a delay at any step can spoil the fruit.
image.caption: A LevlPrep diagram of a banana supply chain.

table.caption: Country B's export earnings by product, 2024 (millions of US dollars; invented data for practice)

items.q: According to the diagram, which step takes place in the importing country?
options: The ripening center, where gas ripens the fruit
The packing house, where fruit is washed and boxed
The port of Guayaquil, where the ship is loaded
The farm, where the bananas are grown and cut

why.correct: Bananas are picked green in Ecuador, shipped cold and ripened near the stores that sell them, in the importing country.
options: Right: the diagram places the ripening center among the steps in the importing country.
The packing house is in Ecuador, the exporting country.
Guayaquil is Ecuador's port, in the exporting country.
The farm is in Ecuador.

items.q: Why does the chain need a refrigerated ship?
options: Bananas grow larger on the ship when kept cold
Cold ships are cheaper than ordinary ships
Bananas spoil fast, so they are kept cool at sea
Importing countries pay a fee for each warm ship

why.correct: Perishable goods need a cold chain from farm to store. Refrigerated shipping is what lets a tropical fruit reach stores thousands of kilometers away.
options: Bananas do not grow after they are cut; cold slows their ripening.
Refrigeration adds cost; it is used because the fruit would spoil without it.
Right: cold storage slows ripening so the fruit survives weeks of shipping.
The diagram gives the reason: spoilage, not fees.

items.q: A student says, "A global supply chain is just the ships and trucks that carry food." Based on the diagram, why is this incomplete?
options: The diagram shows no ships or trucks on its route
The chain ends at the moment the ship reaches the US port
Transport happens before the farm grows the fruit
It also includes growing, packing, ripening and selling

why.correct: Exam readers have docked answers that reduce a supply chain to transport. A global supply chain is every step and place a product passes through, from farm to consumer.
options: It does show a ship and two ports.
The diagram continues to the ripening center and the store.
Transport comes after the fruit is grown and packed.
Right: of seven steps, only some are transport; the others grow, prepare and sell the fruit.

items.q: A strike closes the US port for two weeks. Based on the diagram, what is the most likely effect?
options: Farms in Ecuador grow bananas more slowly
Fruit on waiting ships spoils and US stores run short
Ripening centers in the US speed up their work to catch up
Shoppers in Ecuador pay more for bananas

why.correct: Global supply chains link distant places, so a problem in one place spreads along the chain to others.
options: A US port strike does not change how bananas grow.
Right: a break at one step stops everything after it, and the fruit is perishable.
With no fruit arriving, ripening centers have nothing to ripen.
The fruit was bound for the US; Ecuador may even have extra.

items.q: What percent of Country B's export earnings came from coffee in 2024?

mistakes.why: You found the fraction, 0.6. Multiply by 100 to give a percent.
Divide coffee by the total of all exports (1,000), not by the other products (400).

items.q: Which concept does the table show most clearly?
options: Subsistence agriculture
Economies of scale
Commodity dependence
Domestication

why.correct: Commodity dependence means relying on one or a few raw exports for most export earnings. Coffee alone is 60% of Country B's.
options: Export earnings come from selling abroad; subsistence farming is for the family's own use.
The table shows what a country exports, not costs per unit.
Right: one raw farm product brings in most of the country's export earnings.
Domestication is the change of wild species into crops; the table is about trade.

items.q: If the world price of coffee fell by half, what would most likely happen to Country B?
options: Export earnings would drop sharply, hurting farmers and the budget
Its export earnings would rise because it sells more flowers
Nothing would change, because coffee is a small share of its total exports
Farmers would switch to tea at once with no cost

why.correct: Commodity dependence makes a country vulnerable to price swings it cannot control.
options: Right: with 60% of earnings from coffee, a price crash cuts national income at once.
Flowers are only 12% of exports and nothing suggests they would grow.
Coffee is the largest share by far: 60%.
Coffee trees take years to grow; switching crops is slow and costly.

items.q: Which policy would most reduce Country B's commodity dependence?
options: Planting more coffee on newly cleared land to export more beans
Roasting and packaging coffee at home and growing other exports
Stopping clothing exports to focus on raw coffee
Selling coffee to just one importing country

why.correct: Countries reduce commodity dependence by diversifying exports and by processing raw goods at home so more value stays in the country.
options: That would raise dependence on coffee further.
Right: adding value and diversifying spread earnings across more products.
That narrows exports, raising dependence.
One buyer adds risk; it does not reduce dependence on coffee.
Buying most of a country's food from one supermarket chain
Growing food mainly to feed the farmer's own family
Owning several steps of a commodity chain
Relying on one or a few raw exports for most export earnings

why.correct: UNCTAD calls a country commodity dependent when raw commodities make up more than 60% of its merchandise export earnings.
options: Commodity dependence is about a country's exports, not where shoppers buy food.
That is subsistence agriculture.
That is vertical integration.
Right: for example, a country earning most of its export income from coffee or cocoa.

items.q: Brazil exports more soybeans than any other country, and much of its crop is shipped to China, the largest soybean importer (USDA, 2024). Which statement best describes this link?
options: A global supply chain links farms in Brazil to buyers in China
A local market links farms and buyers in one Brazilian town
Subsistence farms in Brazil feed their own families with soybeans
China grows soybeans in Brazil using shifting cultivation

why.correct: Global supply chains connect producing and consuming regions continents apart. Much of China's soybean imports feed pigs and poultry.
options: Right: soybeans grown in Brazil are shipped across the world to feed livestock in China.
The buyers are in China, on another continent.
These are large commercial farms selling abroad.
Brazilian soybeans are grown on large, fixed commercial farms.

items.q: After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, grain shipments from Ukraine's Black Sea ports were disrupted, and world wheat prices rose. What does this show about the global food system?
options: Food prices depend on local weather alone
Wheat is a subsistence crop that is not traded
Politics and conflict can affect food supply in places far away
Supply chains affect just the countries that grow the crop

why.correct: Food distribution is shaped by politics, trade and transport routes, not just by how much food is grown. A UN and Türkiye brokered deal later let ships sail from July 2022 to July 2023.
options: This case shows politics and conflict affecting prices, not weather alone.
Ukraine is a major wheat exporter; that is why prices moved.
Right: a war in one region raised prices for buyers in other regions that import grain.
Importing countries far from Ukraine felt the price rise.

items.q: The world produces enough calories to feed everyone, yet some people go hungry. Which explanation fits the global food system?
options: The world grows too little food to feed its growing population
Hungry people prefer to grow cash crops for export
Food spoils before it can be grown
Poverty, conflict and poor roads keep food from some people

why.correct: Access depends on income, prices, transport, storage and politics. This is one reason the Green Revolution did not end hunger everywhere.
options: Global output is large enough; the problem is access and distribution.
This does not explain hunger; many hungry people are farmers who lack land, money or markets.
Food spoils after it is grown, during storage and shipping.
Right: hunger is often about who can get food, not about how much is grown.

items.q: Which factors shape how food is distributed around the world? Select all that apply.
options: Trade rules and taxes on imports
Wars and blocked ports or roads
The order of von Thünen's rings around a town
The survey method used to divide farmland
The hearth where a crop was first domesticated

why.correct: Politics, trade rules, transport and income shape food distribution.
options: Right: they change what can be sold where and at what price.
Right: conflict can cut supply chains.
The rings describe local land use, not global distribution.
Survey methods shape field patterns, not world food distribution.
Where a crop began thousands of years ago does not decide where it is sold.

items.q: Cocoa grown on small family farms in Côte d'Ivoire is made into chocolate sold in Europe. How do the effects of a fall in the world cocoa price differ by scale?
options: Nationally nothing changes; locally families earn more
Nationally export earnings fall; locally farm families earn less
Globally chocolate disappears; nationally prices rise
Locally farms grow more cocoa; globally prices rise

why.correct: Explaining across scales: one global price change affects the national economy and household incomes on local farms.
options: A price fall lowers earnings at both scales.
Right: the same price drop cuts national export income and household incomes at the local scale.
A lower cocoa price makes cocoa cheaper, not scarce.
Lower prices give farmers less reason to grow more.

items.q: Build an explanation of a risk of commodity dependence in a named place.

why.correct: Place, commodity and effect, with the link "so".

specific.frame: In ___, export earnings depend heavily on ___, so ___.
specific.model: In Côte d'Ivoire, export earnings depend heavily on cocoa, so a fall in the world cocoa price cuts the income of farm families and the government.

place.label: Place
options: Côte d'Ivoire
a tropical country

why.1: Name the country; a vague place earns no credit.

concept.label: Export
options: cocoa
clothing factories

why.1: The point is a raw farm commodity, such as cocoa.

effect.label: Effect
options: a fall in the world cocoa price cuts the income of farm families and the government
the country can set the world price of cocoa as it wishes

why.1: Exporters of a raw commodity usually take the world price; they cannot set it.
